content: Many journals now publish articles online before they appear in print. The version of an article published online early is considered the final version, and its content will be identical to the version that appears in the print journal. Once the final article is assigned to a specific journal issue, the early online version is removed. Electronic journals are increasingly supplementing or even replacing traditional paper journals. Subscription costs for electronic journals are significantly lower than those for print publications, and in some cases, they are even free. By the end of 1996, there were 306 electronic journals, representing a 70% increase from the previous year, covering fields such as mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, and social sciences. This number has continued to grow. While it is premature to predict the demise of traditional biomedical journals, the tools of scientific communication are undergoing a profound transformation. The World Wide Web has made it inevitable that new systems for disseminating research will partially replace or supplement traditional journals. Publishing peer-reviewed original research online still incurs costs, which are currently covered by subscribers. However, a new model is being tested where authors, their institutions, or their funders pay for the peer review and electronic dissemination of their articles. Experiments with this author pay model are already underway. BioMed Central, an independent commercial publisher, is dedicated to providing free and immediate online access to the full text of peer-reviewed biomedical research. Authors retain copyright of their work. BioMed Central publishes over 90 peer-reviewed journals in biology and medicine and offers free technical support and hosting for groups of researchers who wish to run open-access, peer-reviewed online journals under their own editorial control. The company does not receive support from governments or scientific societies. Instead of charging users, BioMed Central covers the costs of peer review and publication by charging authors a processing fee for their manuscripts. In 2003, this fee was $500 per published article, which could be paid directly by authors, typically from their research funds, or through their institutions via BioMed Central’s membership scheme. That year, BioMed Central had 291 institutional members from 29 countries. The fee is waived for authors from developing countries or those unable to pay. Adopting a $500 charge per published article on a wide scale could result in a tenfold cost saving for science and society. It has been estimated that the scientific community currently pays approximately $5,000 per published article, based on publishers’ gross revenues from journal subscriptions. The Public Library of Science (PLoS), a non-profit organization of scientists and physicians, is another initiative committed to making scientific and medical literature freely available as a public resource. It received a $9 million grant from the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation to fund its first four years. The internet and electronic publishing enable the creation of public libraries of science containing the full text and data of any published research article, available free of charge to anyone, anywhere in the world. To achieve this, a new business model for scientific publishing is required, treating publication costs as the final integral step in funding a research project. To demonstrate the viability of this model for publishing high-quality research, PLoS launched its first peer-reviewed journal, PLoS Biology, on October 13, 2003, in both print and online formats. PLoS Medicine followed in 2004. PLoS Biology plans to cover its costs by charging authors $1,500 per published paper. Once accepted for publication, the article is made immediately and freely available online. Researchers are required to report regularly to funding agencies on the progress of their research, with most agencies requiring annual progress reports and some requiring six-monthly reports. In multi-year projects, funding for the next period is contingent on the submission of a satisfactory progress report and a financial report detailing expenditures during the covered period. Progress reports should provide sufficient information to satisfy the agency about the project’s progress, outline plans for the next period, and address any encountered problems. Any submitted, accepted, or published papers should be mentioned. If the research did not proceed as scheduled, investigators may request a no-cost extension of the grant. At the end of the grant, a more detailed final report, including a final financial report, is expected to close the grant. Researchers have a collective responsibility to ensure that healthcare providers have access to scientific evidence tailored to their needs. Passive dissemination of information is insufficient to keep health professionals’ knowledge up to date. While skills in searching for and critically appraising evidence are essential, most health professionals cannot keep pace with the rapid growth of scientific knowledge. Approximately two million medical articles are published annually. A 1995 editorial in the British Medical Journal estimated that doctors would need to read about 17 articles daily, every day of the year, to stay current in their specialty. Most research findings first appear in peer-reviewed journals, but the small number of studies with practical implications for health professionals are scattered across numerous publications. These findings need to be synthesized. Researchers should actively communicate new information to health professionals in a manner tailored to their needs. Evidence-based reviews and clinical practice guidelines are examples of effective communication methods. Evidence-based reviews rigorously evaluate important papers and present the results in a format that busy health professionals can easily understand. For example, the journal Evidence-Based Medicine, a collaboration between the American College of Physicians and the BMJ Publishing Group, includes abstracts and commentaries from various specialties, focusing on studies addressing common clinical conditions. It also publishes systematic reviews and editorials of general interest. Systematic reviews, such as those conducted by the Cochrane Collaboration, have become valuable resources. Clinical practice guidelines, developed after exhaustive evidence reviews by professional organizations, translate complex research findings into actionable recommendations for clinical practice. These guidelines balance the strengths and limitations of relevant research evidence with the practical realities of healthcare settings. They also acknowledge uncertainty, as evidence does not always lead to clear recommendations. Recommendations are often graded based on the level of evidence supporting them, ranging from strong evidence (Grade A) to insufficient evidence (Grade C) or evidence against the recommendation (Grade E). Health policymakers require scientifically validated information to make evidence-based decisions. Researchers have a responsibility to communicate policy-relevant findings to policymakers. Publishing a study or sending a report is insufficient; face-to-face presentations with time for discussion are more effective. Grant-making bodies often allocate funds for disseminating research results, which may include meetings with health managers and policymakers to discuss findings. Communication with policymakers should ideally begin during the research planning stage to ensure that research questions are appropriately framed and tested in relevant contexts. Presentations to policymakers should be tailored to the audience, avoid technical jargon, and focus on conclusions and recommendations. Specific, actionable recommendations are more likely to be implemented than general ones. Visual aids can highlight key points, and adequate time should be allowed for discussion. An executive summary of the study should be provided, as it is more likely to be read than the full report. The health research community has an obligation to ensure that patients have access to scientifically valid and understandable information. The internet has led to an explosion of health information, with over 100,000 medical websites of varying quality. This revolution is driven by consumer demand for online health resources. Efforts like MEDLINEplus, launched by the National Library of Medicine, direct consumers to scientifically sound resources for researching health questions. Care must be taken when communicating research findings to patients, as poorly presented information can lead to confusion and incorrect decisions. For example, women over 50 may be told that mammography reduces their risk of dying from breast cancer by 25%, but few would understand that this translates to an absolute risk reduction of only one in 1,000. Clear communication is essential to empower patients with valid and comprehensible information. If research involves a community-based study, the community has a right to know the outcomes. Investigators should share findings with the community before making them public, ensuring that the community agrees with the conclusions and addressing any additional questions.
